 SPF, Actually – Part 1: What SPF 50 means and how to use it properly 
 Published by capeetc on November 7, 2026 
 Tweet #CapeTownETC 
 Share 
 -->
 It’s a Saturday morning at the foot of Lion’s Head. Your sunscreen says SPF 50, so you squeeze out a modest blob, rub it over your face and set off. Most of us treat that number as ‘sorted for the day’, but it means something narrower than it sounds. A 2014 review found people typically apply only 20 to 50% of the amount needed to reach the labelled SPF.
 This is Part 1 of SPF, Actually , a short series that makes sun protection easier to understand, one everyday question at a time. Each part stands alone, so you can start here.
 What the number measures 
 SPF stands for sun protection factor. It measures the amount of UVB protection, and UVB is the type of ultraviolet radiation most responsible for sunburn.
 The scale is not what it looks like. A dermatologist quoted by PBS NewsHour explains that SPF 30 filters about 97% of UVB rays and SPF 50 about 98%. Doubling the SPF does not mean the sunscreen protects twice as well.
 The sun here is strong enough to make the details count. A review by the South African Medical Research Council and the University of Pretoria notes that the UV index in South Africa can reach 13 in summer, and 11 or above is considered extreme. It helps to know your real UV risk before you head out.
 What the evidence says 
 Lab versus real life. The 2014 review notes that SPF is tested at a thickness of 2 mg per cm², but people usually apply about 0.39 to 1.0 mg per cm². A thin layer of SPF 50 therefore gives you less than the label promises.
 Myth: a higher SPF lasts longer. It doesn’t. MD Anderson Cancer Center advises that whatever SPF you choose, you should reapply every two hours, or after sweating or swimming.
 Myth: SPF covers everything. SPF tells you only about UVB, not UVA, which is also harmful. The NHS says the label should show an SPF of at least 30 and at least 4-star UVA protection. South Africa’s sunscreen standard, SANS 1557, covers labelling and packaging requirements. CANSA says its Seal of Recognition programme has required an SPF between 20 and 50 and broad-spectrum protection since 2005. That statement dates from 2012, so check the current criteria.
 So is SPF 50 worth buying? Yes, as a safety margin rather than a licence to stay out longer. NHS inform suggests that if you worry you aren’t applying enough, you could use a stronger sunscreen, such as SPF 50 instead of SPF 30. The American Cancer Society, the A merican Academy of Dermatology (AAD) and the NHS all recommend at least SPF 30, alongside shade and clothing.
 Step by step: using SPF 50 properly 
 Read the label. Look for broad-spectrum (UVA and UVB) protection and SPF 30 or higher. The CANSA Seal is one local quality marker.
 Choose SPF 50 for long days outdoors or if you tend to apply lightly. SPF 30 is a sound everyday minimum.
 Measure it out. The AAD says most adults need about 1 ounce, roughly a shot glass, to cover skin not covered by clothing. NHS inform gives around 35 ml, or 6 to 8 teaspoons. For your face, use at least 1 teaspoon.
 Apply early. The AAD says it takes about 15 minutes for sunscreen to protect you. NHS inform suggests 30 minutes before going out.
 Cover the forgotten spots. That means neck, face, ears, tops of feet and legs. If your hair is thinning, apply sunscreen to your scalp or wear a wide-brimmed hat.
 Reapply every two hours , and straight after being in water, even if the product is water resistant, and after towel drying or sweating.
 Add shade, a hat and sunglasses between late morning and mid-afternoon.
 A practical plan for a Cape Town day 
 Before you leave 
 Apply at home, on dry skin, before you pack the car for Camps Bay or Kirstenbosch.
 Check the expiry date. The AAD notes that people who get sunburnt usually didn’t reapply, used too little, or used an expired sunscreen.
 Put the bottle and a hat in your bag, not in the boot.
 While you’re out 
 Set a two-hour phone alarm. The American Cancer Society suggests this: set an alarm or timer to remind you to reapply at least every 2 hours.
 Trust the clock, not your skin. A south-easter cools you down and can hide how much sun you’re getting.
 Top up after a swim at Muizenberg or a sweaty climb up Platteklip Gorge.
 Afterwards 
 Note how much you used. A 200 ml bottle holds only five or six full-body applications at 35 ml each, so one that lasts all summer is probably being under-used.
 Common mistakes to avoid 
 Treating SPF 50 as ’50 times longer’. Reapply every two hours regardless of the number.
 Using a thin layer. Measure it out the first few times until you can judge the amount by eye.
 Applying once, at home, then not again. Reapplication is part of how sunscreen works in practice.
 Waiting until you reach the beach. The AAD warns that if you apply it once you’re in the sun, your skin is unprotected and can burn.
 Ignoring UVA. A high SPF with no broad-spectrum claim leaves a gap. Check the label.
 Relying on sunscreen alone. Shade and clothing do much of the work.
 Who needs extra care 
 Fair skin burns fastest. MD Anderson says a higher SPF may be relatively more beneficial for fairer skin, but nobody should skip sunscreen, and a broad-spectrum SPF 30 gives good protection for everyone. Darker skin still needs sunscreen.
 Babies and children. The AAD says infants and toddlers 6 months and older may use a broad-spectrum, water-resistant SPF 30 or higher on skin not covered by clothing. NHS inform advises keeping children under 6 months out of direct strong sunlight.
 Medicines and skin conditions. Some medicines make skin more sun-sensitive. Ask your pharmacist whether yours do.
 When to see a doctor or pharmacist 
 A pharmacist can help with mild sunburn. The NHS says you can ask a pharmacist about the best sunburn treatments and whether you need to see a GP.
 Get urgent medical help, from a GP or a casualty unit, if you’ve been in the sun and have blistered or swollen skin, a very high temperature or feeling hot and shivery, dizziness, sickness, headache or muscle cramps. The same applies if your baby or young child has sunburn. A headache after a day outside is worth taking seriously, and our guide on when a headache needs a doctor covers the wider picture.
 Check your skin about once a month. The American Cancer Society’s ABCDE guide flags a mole that is uneven, has ragged edges, has uneven colour or is changing in size, shape or colour. See your GP or a dermatologist about anything new, changing or unusual.
 Key takeaways 
 SPF measures UVB protection only: SPF 30 filters about 97% and SPF 50 about 98%.
 A higher SPF does not last longer. Reapply every two hours.
 Under-applying is the biggest gap between the label and real protection, so measure out a shot glass for the body and a teaspoon for the face.
 Choose broad-spectrum, SPF 30 or higher, and pick SPF 50 for long days or light applicators.
 Use shade, a hat and clothing as well, and see a doctor for blistering, fever or changing moles.
